newsitem.title: PERU: U.S. woman "terrorist" in Peru jail wants retrial.
newsitem.headline: U.S. woman "terrorist" in Peru jail wants retrial.

text.p: Lori Berenson, an American woman jailed for life in Peru as a terrorist, says she is innocent and wants a retrial, according to her parents who visited her for the first time in a year.

They said she told them she was innocent of the "preposterous charges," and urged them to keep pressing for a civil trial when they visited her late on Saturday at the grim Yanamayo maximum security prison in the 13,000-foot (4,000-metre) high Andean city of Puno.
"She asked us 'Are you still pressing for a civil trial? It's really important I have a fair trial,'" her mother Rhoda Berenson said directly after their 30-minute meeting, separated by a mesh wire.

Lori Berenson spends 23-1/2 hours a day in a cold, tiny cell with a hole for a toilet and no furniture. She receives insufficient food, has laryngitis and suffers altitude-related ailments such as dizziness, her parents said.
"It's like living in a refigerator up there. It's incredible how humanity survives," said Rhoda Berenson. "But she told us 'Listen, don't worry about me.'"

Berenson, 27, was sentenced in January by a "faceless" military court for allegedly helping plot a takeover of Peru's Congress by the Cuban-inspired guerrilla group, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Since her conviction on charges of treason, there has been a growing campaign in the United States, actively supported by former President Jimmy Carter, to annul the decison of the secret court, where judges and lawyers wore hoods and cross-examination was not allowed.
Diplomatic pressure from Washington also led Peru's President Alberto Fujimori to say he was considering a deal in which Berenson could be transferred to the United States.
President Bill Clinton has also asked Peru to review the "due process" in the case and 87 U.S. congressmen and 20 senators have signed letters urging Fujimori to order a civil trial.
"We are encouraged to fight on," said Rhoda Berenson. "I think she won't be spending the rest of her life there. In Peru, like much of South America, nothing is forever."

The Peruvian military's conviction was based on accusations that Berenson was a leader of the MRTA, renting a house in Lima as a front for the guerrillas, transporting arms, helping to psychologically prepare rebel fighters, and gathering intelligence by posing as a journalist for U.S.-based magazines.

Her parents, who under Peruvian law had to wait a year before visiting, said her hands were "grotesque" because of circulation problems caused by the altitude. But because of a storm that brought an electrical blackout in Puno, they could not tell in the dim light how severe her weight loss was.
Berenson's parents brought food and books from New York for their daughter who gave them cards and knitted Christmas presents to take back to family.
"I was surprised and relieved. She didn't look terrible. She's very courageous," her father Mark Berenson said, crying as he showed a traditional Andean hat his daughter made him.
